section.title: Zophar's Second Speech
section.sectionRationale: Stung by Job's warning that his accusers should fear judgment themselves, Zophar answers with his most vivid speech, insisting the triumph of the wicked has always been brief. His central image, sweetness in the mouth that turns to venom in the belly, captures the friends' whole theology: sin's pleasures are real but always, inevitably, short-lived and self-destructive.
section.thesis: Zophar doubles down on the friends' conviction that the wicked's prosperity is fleeting and their gains poisonous, painting a vivid, almost visceral picture of ill-gotten wealth turning to venom, a truth that is often accurate in general even as its aim at Job continues to miss the mark entirely.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Zophar's agitated reply, provoked by Job's warning, restating that the wicked's joy has always been brief; his image of the wicked man perishing like his own dung after a moment's exaltation; his central picture of sin's sweetness turning to the venom of cobras in the wicked man's stomach; and his closing declaration that the heavens themselves will expose the wicked man's iniquity on the day of God's wrath.

units.label: The triumph of the wicked is brief

verses.text: Then Zophar the Naamathite replied:
"So my anxious thoughts compel me to answer, because of the turmoil within me.
I have heard a rebuke that insults me, and my understanding prompts a reply.
Do you not know that from antiquity, since man was placed on the earth,
the triumph of the wicked has been brief and the joy of the godless momentary?

units.label: He perishes like his own dung
units.note: he will be chased away like a vision in the night

verses.text: "Though his arrogance reaches the heavens, and his head touches the clouds,
he will perish forever, like his own dung; those who had seen him will ask, 'Where is he?'
He will fly away like a dream, never to be found; he will be chased away like a vision in the night.
The eye that saw him will see him no more, and his place will no longer behold him.
His sons will seek the favor of the poor, for his own hands must return his wealth.
The youthful vigor that fills his bones will lie down with him in the dust.

units.label: Sweet in his mouth, venom in his stomach
units.note: the venom of cobras within him

verses.text: "Though evil is sweet in his mouth and he conceals it under his tongue,
though he cannot bear to let it go and keeps it in his mouth,
yet in his stomach his food sours into the venom of {{pethen|cobras}} within him.
He {{bala|swallows}} wealth but vomits it out; God will force it from his stomach.
He will suck the poison of cobras; the fangs of a viper will kill him.
He will not enjoy the streams, the rivers flowing with honey and cream.
He must return the fruit of his labor without consuming it; he cannot enjoy the profits of his trading.
For he has oppressed and forsaken the poor; he has seized houses he did not build.

units.label: The heavens will expose his iniquity

verses.text: "Because his appetite is never satisfied, he cannot escape with his treasure.
Nothing is left for him to consume; thus his prosperity will not endure.
In the midst of his plenty, he will be distressed; the full force of misery will come upon him.

When he has filled his stomach, God will vent His fury upon him, 
raining it down on him as he eats.
Though he flees from an iron weapon, a bronze-tipped arrow will pierce him.

It is drawn out of his back, the gleaming point from his liver. 
Terrors come over him.

Total darkness is reserved for his treasures. A fire unfanned will consume him 
and devour what is left in his tent.
The heavens will expose his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him.
The possessions of his house will be removed, flowing away on the day of {{chemah|God's wrath}}.
This is the wicked man's {{nachalah|portion}} from God, the inheritance God has appointed him."

pethen.gloss: A venomous serpent, often translated cobra or asp. Zophar's image of a man's stolen sweetness souring into the venom of cobras in his own stomach is a vivid picture of sin's self-destructive nature, poison the sinner has effectively swallowed himself.

bala.gloss: To swallow, engulf, or devour. Zophar pictures the wicked man swallowing wealth greedily only to have God force it back out of him, an image of ill-gotten gain that cannot ultimately be kept or digested.

chemah.gloss: Heat, fury, wrath, often used of God's righteous anger against sin. Zophar's closing reference to the day of God's chemah pictures divine judgment as an unavoidable, burning reckoning awaiting the unrepentant wicked.

nachalah.gloss: Inheritance, portion, allotted share. Zophar closes by calling the wicked man's ruin his nachalah, his appointed inheritance from God, a bitter irony on a word usually associated with covenant blessing and land given to God's people.

basic.context: Stung by Job's warning in the previous chapter that his accusers should themselves fear judgment, Zophar answers with agitation, insisting that history itself proves the triumph of the wicked is always brief. He paints a vivid, almost visceral picture: sin tastes sweet at first, concealed under the tongue, but sours in the stomach into the venom of cobras, forcing the wicked man to vomit up everything he swallowed. He closes with a sweeping vision of the heavens themselves exposing the wicked man's guilt and God's wrath sweeping away everything he owns, calling this ruin the wicked man's very inheritance from God.
basic.hermeneutics: Zophar's underlying conviction, that sin's pleasures are real but always short-lived and ultimately self-destructive, is broadly true and echoed throughout wisdom literature. The persistent error, again, is applying this general truth as a diagnosis of Job's specific suffering, with no evidence beyond the assumption that catastrophic suffering must prove hidden, ill-gotten gain, an assumption the reader already knows is false in Job's case.
basic.originalLanguages: Zophar's central image turns on pethen, venomous cobras, into which the wicked man's sweet, secret sin sours once swallowed, bala. His closing warning names the day of chemah, God's burning wrath, and calls the wicked man's utter ruin his nachalah, portion or inheritance, a bitter twist on a word normally associated with covenant blessing.
basic.typology: Zophar's picture of sin as sweet in the mouth but venomous in the stomach anticipates the biblical pattern of sin's deceitfulness, promising pleasure while delivering death, a pattern fully exposed and finally defeated only through Christ, who bore sin's true venom on behalf of His people.
basic.christ: Zophar rightly says sin's sweetness sours into poison, echoing the biblical pattern that the wages of sin is death; where Zophar can only picture inevitable, self-inflicted ruin for the sinner, the gospel offers a different, gracious reversal: Christ Himself drank the cup of God's wrath, the chemah Zophar describes, so that those who trust Him receive life instead of the poisoned inheritance sin actually deserves.
basic.god: God is presented here as the one who forces the ill-gotten gain back out of the wicked man's stomach and rains fury down upon him, a real and true picture of divine justice against unrepentant sin in general. The chapter's ongoing error is treating Job, whom the reader knows to be innocent, as though he were this very case study in deserved, self-inflicted ruin.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 6:23 says the wages of sin is death, echoing Zophar's picture of sin's ultimately fatal harvest; Proverbs 20:17 says bread gained by deceit tastes sweet, but the mouth ends up full of gravel; Isaiah 51:17 pictures drinking the cup of the LORD's wrath, an image Christ Himself would take up in Gethsemane.
basic.oneStory: Zophar's vivid picture of sin's sweetness turning to venom is broadly true and echoed throughout Scripture's teaching on sin's deceitfulness, yet wrongly aimed once more at an innocent man. The gospel answers the very wrath Zophar describes: Christ drinks that cup of judgment Himself, so that those who trust Him inherit blessing rather than the poisoned portion sin actually earns.

context.literary:
Zophar is the only one of the three friends who does not get a third speech, so this is his last word, and he spends it on a single picture. The speech is built like a tour of the body. The wicked man's arrogance touches the clouds in verse 6, but from verse 11 the poem descends into the bones, then the mouth and tongue, the stomach, the belly, the back and the liver. Sin enters at the lips, is savoured under the tongue, and does its damage inside. Nothing about the ruin is public at first; it happens where no one can see.

The movement has three parts of unequal weight. Verses 4 to 11 are about disappearance: he is gone like a dream, and even his sons must pay back what he took. Verses 12 to 19 are the centre of gravity, the slow taste of sweetness turning to poison, and only here does Zophar name a crime, in verse 19, oppressing the poor and seizing houses he did not build. Verses 20 to 29 then reverse the direction, from inside out. What was hidden in the body is now exposed to the whole cosmos, and the heavens and the earth themselves rise as witnesses, verse 27.

The speech is also framed. Verse 5 says the triumph of the wicked is brief, and verse 29 closes by calling all of this the wicked man's portion from God. Between them Zophar keeps returning to eating and swallowing, so that appetite becomes the governing metaphor: the man who cannot be satisfied is consumed by the very thing he devours.

Two things set this speech apart from the others. Zophar begins by admitting he is agitated, verses 2 and 3, which none of the other friends do so openly, so the speech is more heat than argument. And the wicked man is drawn entirely in the third person, with no address to Job. That is how the friends hurt: the portrait never names Job, yet it comes after Job's own warning in 19:28-29 and sits in the mouth of a man who has plainly decided who the portrait fits.
context.historical:
Zophar is called the Naamathite, and the book gives no reliable way to place his home. What matters historically is the world he speaks from, a patriarchal society where wealth was flocks, land and houses, and where a man who built up an estate by force was a familiar figure. The sin Zophar names is land seizure and the ruin of the poor, verse 19, the same offence the Law later forbids when it says not to move a neighbour's boundary marker, Deuteronomy 19:14, and which the prophets will hammer, Isaiah 5:8 and Micah 2:1-2.

Zophar's language of honey and cream, verse 17, is the language of the promised land. Israel's hearers knew a land flowing with milk and honey, Exodus 3:8, and they knew the covenant curses that reverse it, Deuteronomy 28:30-33, where a man builds a house he will not live in and plants a vineyard he will not enjoy, and strangers eat the fruit of his labour. Zophar takes the shape of those curses and applies it as a law of nature to every wicked man.

The snake imagery would have been immediate to anyone who lived near the desert. Venomous snakes kill by poison working inside the body, which fits the way Zophar imagines sin working, and the same picture of cobra poison appears in the Song of Moses, Deuteronomy 32:32-33, and in Psalm 58:3-4. The picture of an arrow drawn out through the back and the liver, verse 25, is a battlefield image, and 'gall' is the Hebrew idiom for the liver's bitter fluid, as the BSB footnote on verse 25 notes: 'Literally from his gall.'

The appeal to what has always been true 'from antiquity,' verse 4, is the typical move of the ancient wise man. Knowledge is inherited, tested by generations, and hard to argue against. That is why Job's counter-evidence in the next chapter is so disruptive: he answers tradition with what he has watched with his own eyes.
context.canonical:
Zophar's central proverb has a real home in Scripture. 'Food gained by fraud is sweet to a man, but later his mouth is full of gravel,' Proverbs 20:17. The lips of the forbidden woman 'drip honey,' but 'in the end she is bitter as wormwood,' Proverbs 5:3-4, and the invitation that 'Stolen water is sweet' ends among the dead, Proverbs 9:17-18. The Psalms tell the worried believer not to fret at the wicked, for 'they wither quickly like grass,' Psalm 37:1-2, and in Psalm 37:35-36 the poet says he saw a wicked man flourishing like a tree, and later he was gone, 'though I searched, he could not be found,' which is very close to Zophar's 'Where is he?' in verse 7.

Habakkuk gives an oracle against the man who 'amasses what is not his,' and promises that his victims will one day taunt him, Habakkuk 2:6-9. That is Zophar's picture in prophetic form, but the prophet does not say every rich man is such a man.

Job itself shows the limit. Job 27:13 repeats nearly word for word 'This is the wicked man's portion from God,' so the book lets Job agree with the shape of Zophar's warning while refusing its use as an accusation. In the end God says the friends have not spoken accurately of Him, Job 42:7.

The New Testament takes up the same wisdom without Zophar's mistake. Jesus tells of the rich man whose barns were full and whose life was required that night, Luke 12:16-21. James addresses the rich whose withheld wages are 'crying out against' them, James 5:1-6. And John's sweet-then-bitter scroll, Revelation 10:9-10, borrows the same taste sequence, though there it is God's word that is sweet and bitter, not sin.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author of Job wanted his readers to hear Zophar at full strength, not to dismiss him as a fool. This speech is well made, its images are sound, and much of it is what Proverbs and the Psalms also say. That is exactly the danger the book is exploring: a true principle, delivered with confidence and vivid detail, can still be a false word to the man in front of you. The first hearers already knew Job was blameless from the prologue, 1:8 and 2:3, so they were meant to feel the gap between Zophar's certainty and Job's reality.

Zophar's speech also reveals its own motive. He begins with anxiety and a sense of insult, verses 2 and 3, and the whole portrait is in the third person, so he never has to say 'you.' The author wants readers to notice how easily the defence of a system becomes personal, and how a man who cannot bear to be corrected will use a beautiful truth to silence someone else.

There is a further purpose. By giving the friends the best available case, the author prepares the way for the answer that comes from the whirlwind. If even this eloquent, biblically shaped account of justice fails to explain Job, then justice cannot be reduced to a formula and the reader must look to God Himself, not to a theory about God.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what one friend believes, and it is not a divine description of how the world always works. God does not endorse Zophar's speech; He rebukes the friends at the end of the book, Job 42:7. So verses like 'his prosperity will not endure,' verse 21, are not promises to be claimed against a particular neighbour or rival.

What the chapter does teach by example is real. Ill-gotten gain does bring ruin, and the New Testament confirms that greed leads people into 'many foolish and harmful desires that plunge them into ruin,' 1 Timothy 6:9-10. It is fair to hear Zophar as a warning to the one who is tempted to take what is not his.

It is not fair to turn the same words into a diagnosis of someone else's suffering. The believer who meets a sick, bereaved or bankrupt person is to weep with them, not to search their history for a cause. Zophar shows what happens when a warning meant for the conscience is aimed at another person's pain.

debates.question: Is Zophar right that the wicked man's ruin is certain and swift, or is he half right?

views.label: Right in principle, wrong in application
views.case: Proverbs 10:2 says 'Ill-gotten treasures profit nothing,' and Psalm 37:35-36 describes a wicked man who flourished and then vanished. Zophar states a moral truth in a strong form, and his mistake is only in aiming it at Job. On this view the chapter is a sound sermon delivered to the wrong man.

views.label: Half right, and wrong as a rule
views.case: Zophar says the triumph of the wicked has always been brief, verses 4 and 5, yet Job answers in 21:7-13 with cases where it was not. Psalm 73:2-5, Jeremiah 12:1-2 and Ecclesiastes 8:14 all wrestle with the same exceptions. On this reading Zophar is wrong that the pattern is universal or that judgment is always visible.

debates.bearing: Both views are partly true, and the book wants us to hold them together. Wickedness is self destructive and God does judge, but not always on a schedule we can see, which is why the next chapter matters so much.

debates.question: Does the wicked man's children 'pay back' the wealth, verse 10, mean judgment falls on descendants?

views.label: Judgment reaches the family
views.case: Verse 10 says his sons 'will seek the favor of the poor,' and verse 28 says 'the possessions of his house will be removed.' Exodus 34:7 speaks of iniquity visited on later generations, and the friends assume the household shares the fate.

views.label: Restitution, not punishment of the innocent
views.case: Ezekiel 18:20 says a son 'will not bear the iniquity of his father.' On this reading the sons in verse 10 are simply left to make amends because the wealth was never legitimately theirs, as restitution laws would require, not because they are punished for his sin.

debates.bearing: The text itself is ambiguous, but Job will press the point in 21:19 and ask why God should store up punishment for children. The safest reading is that Zophar means loss of ill-gotten goods, and the book warns against turning that into a rule about family guilt.

study.originalLanguages:
Zophar's most famous image rests on a snake word. The pethen is a cobra, and in verses 14 and 16 the wicked man's food turns into the venom of cobras and he sucks their poison. The same creature appears in Psalm 58:3-4, where the wicked are compared to a cobra that shuts its ears, and in the Song of Moses, where the poison of cobras is the wine of Israel's enemies, Deuteronomy 32:32-33. That last passage is worth reading beside this chapter, because the Song of Moses also describes a grape-vine that grows from Sodom and turns bitter, the same sweetness-to-poison movement.

A second word plays on heat. The Hebrew chemah can mean burning anger, but it can also mean venom, the burning poison of a snake, and both senses meet in Deuteronomy 32:33 and Psalm 58:4. Whether or not Zophar intends the pun in Job 20, the chapter is about a poison that works like fire, and about God's fury that comes as an answer to it. English readers cannot hear that overlap.

The verb for swallowing, bala, gives the chapter its shape, since verse 15 says he swallows wealth and then vomits it out. The same pair of verbs is used when the fish swallows Jonah and then the LORD commands it to vomit him out, Jonah 1:17 and 2:10, and when the earth swallows the men who rebelled against Moses, Numbers 16:30. Wealth taken in by force is treated as something the body will reject, and the phrase 'God will force it from his stomach' makes God the one who commands the reversal. Proverbs 23:8 uses the vomit picture for a meal wrongly eaten.

Verse 17 speaks of 'streams, the rivers flowing with honey and cream.' The honey belongs to the vocabulary of the promised land, Exodus 3:8, but here the wicked man can only look at the river. Zophar has taken covenant blessing and made it an image of what the wicked will never taste.

The last word of the speech, nachalah, is the ordinary word for inherited land, for the portion assigned to each tribe and the thing Naboth would not sell, 1 Kings 21:3. Zophar calls ruin the wicked man's nachalah, 'the inheritance God has appointed him,' verse 29, turning the loveliest word of family belonging into an image of what he is heir to. Job 27:13 uses nearly identical English in the BSB, 'the wicked man's portion from God, the heritage the ruthless receive,' which shows the phrase became common wisdom vocabulary.

Lastly, verse 25 is a small lesson in translation. The Hebrew of 'the gleaming point from his liver' has the word for gall, and the BSB footnote says 'Literally from his gall.' The arrow that passes through the liver is drawn out with the bitter fluid, so that even the wound repeats the theme of bitterness inside the body.

typology.type: The poisoned cup and the venom of serpents, Job 20:14-16
typology.fulfillment: Zophar's serpent venom matches the picture in Numbers 21:6-9, where the LORD sends venomous snakes among a rebellious people and many die. The escalation comes in Christ: the remedy God gave was a bronze serpent lifted up on a pole, and Jesus says 'so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life,' John 3:14-15. The poison of sin is met not by a formula but by looking at the one lifted up. The type falls short because the bronze snake was only a sign, while the cross is the actual place where the poison was borne.

Scripture often calls God's judgment a cup that the wicked must drink to the dregs, Psalm 75:8 and Isaiah 51:17. Zophar's picture of fury raining down 'as he eats' belongs with that cup. In Gethsemane Jesus prays 'let this cup pass from Me,' and then 'not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39. The one man who had taken no unjust gain drank what Zophar says only the oppressor drinks. The escalation is that the cup passes to Christ so that it may be taken from those who believe. The type falls short because Zophar's cup is retribution for the wicked, while Christ's cup is substitution.

typology.type: Restitution instead of vomiting up, Job 20:18
typology.fulfillment: Zophar says the wicked man must return the fruit of his labour, unconsumed. Zacchaeus does the same thing voluntarily: 'half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold,' Luke 19:8. The forced return of verse 18 becomes a glad restitution after meeting Jesus. The correspondence is not a strict type but a contrast within a pattern: what judgment takes by force, grace can draw out freely. It falls short because Zacchaeus's repayment did not save him, since salvation had already come to his house, Luke 19:9.

typology.type: The rich man whose barns were full, Job 20:20-23
typology.fulfillment: The rich fool of Luke 12:16-21 stores up grain, says 'Take it easy,' and is told 'This very night your life will be required of you.' That is Zophar's verse 22 and 23 in a parable: distress in the midst of plenty, and God speaking as the eater fills his stomach. Jesus does not claim that every wealthy man is a fool, but He uses the same rhythm of abundance and sudden reckoning. The escalation is that Jesus adds the positive alternative, being 'rich toward God,' Luke 12:21, which Zophar never offers.

study.christ:
Zophar's speech leads to Christ most clearly by contrast, and the contrast begins in verse 19. The wicked man 'has oppressed and forsaken the poor,' and 'seized houses he did not build.' Jesus is the opposite in every particular. He had no house of His own, Luke 9:58, yet He gave sight, food and healing to the poor and told them the kingdom was theirs, Luke 6:20. The man Zophar describes takes what he did not build; Christ gives what He did not owe, and He does so to those who cannot repay Him.

The speech leads to Christ by the cup. Zophar says that when the wicked man has filled his stomach, 'God will vent His fury upon him, raining it down on him as he eats,' verse 23. Scripture treats such fury as a cup, Isaiah 51:17 and Psalm 75:8, and Jesus takes up the language Himself, 'let this cup pass from Me,' Matthew 26:39. Paul says God made Him 'to be sin' for us and that He became a curse, 2 Corinthians 5:21 and Galatians 3:13. What Zophar says the oppressor must swallow, the sinless Son swallowed on behalf of others. The sweetness of sin ends in bitterness, but that bitterness was tasted by Christ so that it need not be tasted by everyone who trusts Him.

There is a second pattern. Zophar says 'those who had seen him will ask, Where is he?' and the eye that saw him will see him no more, verses 7 and 9. That is a verdict on the wicked, gone and forgotten. The Gospel account of Christ inverts it. When the women looked for Him at the tomb, the angel said 'He is not here; He is risen,' Luke 24:6, and He was seen by many, Acts 1:3. The one who was numbered with the wicked, Isaiah 53:12, did not vanish like a dream; He was raised so that those who saw Him could tell what they saw.

The speech also exposes what Christ does not do. Zophar assumes that suffering proves guilt. When His disciples asked whose sin caused a man's blindness, Jesus answered that neither he nor his parents had sinned, John 9:2-3. Job stands as a man in this same position, and the Gospels show Jesus refusing the equation that Zophar defends. Christ Himself suffered without any wickedness in Him, so suffering can no longer be read as a verdict on the sufferer.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Zophar is not a prophet of Christ, and his words are not a coded prophecy of Gethsemane. The links here rest on the Bible's own repeated cup language, on Christ's own words, and on the shape of a world in which grace answers judgment. The gospel takes Zophar's truth about sin's poison seriously, which is why it needs a cross, and it rejects his application, which is why it also has room for the innocent sufferer.
study.god:
The first thing this speech shows about God is that He is the one who decides what sin will taste like in the end. Verse 15 says 'God will force it from his stomach,' and verse 23 says God vents His fury. Zophar sees an active hand behind the ruin of the wicked, and Scripture agrees that God is not indifferent to how wealth is gained. Proverbs 22:22-23 says 'the LORD will take up their case' against those who rob the poor. A God who cares who owns a field and who sleeps in a cloak is the God of Sinai, and Zophar is right to say so.

The speech also shows God as a witness. Verse 27 says 'The heavens will expose his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him.' Creation is not neutral. Earlier in the book Job cries 'O earth, do not cover my blood,' 16:18, and Genesis 4:10 has Abel's blood crying out from the ground. God has built a world in which wrong is heard by the sky and the soil, and He can call them as witnesses, Psalm 97:6.

Yet the passage holds a tension that Zophar cannot see. He speaks confidently of God's wrath, but the God the book describes is also 'compassionate,' Exodus 22:27, patient and kind so that people will repent, Romans 2:4-5, and slow to strike. Zophar has only one attribute in view, justice, and he has made it fast and mechanical. The prologue shows another side, since God is the one who says Job is blameless, 1:8 and 2:3, and it will be the God of Zophar's speech who says at the end that Zophar has not spoken about Him accurately, 42:7.

So the doctrine of God being shaped here is a doctrine that includes both hatred of oppression and freedom from formula. God is just, and He judges what is stolen from the poor. He is also free, and He is not bound to run His justice on a timetable that lets one friend judge another. When Zophar says the wicked man's prosperity 'will not endure,' he is right that God has no patience for a system built on the ruin of others, and wrong that God's time is his time.

For worship this means two things. First, it is right to bring the taste of injustice to God, to name what was seized and ask Him to answer, because He hears the cry of those who are crushed. Second, it is right to be wary of using His wrath as a weapon against anyone. The one who prays about the wicked must leave room for God, as Paul says, 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay,' Romans 12:19. Zophar's mistake is to take that room away.

crossReferences.note: Food gained by fraud is sweet at first and then the mouth is full of gravel. This is the proverb behind Zophar's picture, and it shows he speaks from real wisdom. The difference is that the proverb states a pattern for the conscience, and Zophar turns it into a proof about a particular man's suffering.

The lips of the forbidden woman drip honey, but in the end she is bitter as wormwood. The sweetness-then-bitterness sequence is the same as verses 12 to 14, applied to adultery rather than theft, which shows how general the wisdom pattern was in Israel.

The Song of Moses speaks of a vine from Sodom whose grapes are poisonous and whose wine is 'the venom of serpents, the deadly poison of cobras.' The vocabulary is the same as Zophar's cobras in verses 14 and 16, so his imagery has a covenant background: this is what a people gets when it turns from the LORD.

The psalmist saw a wicked, ruthless man flourishing like a well-rooted tree, then found he was gone, though he searched. That is Zophar's 'Where is he?' in verse 7, but the psalm is offered as comfort to those who wait on the LORD, not as an accusation.

Job himself later says 'This is the wicked man's portion from God,' echoing Zophar's closing line in 20:29. So the book lets both men agree on the fate of the oppressor. Their disagreement is not about that fate but about whether it explains Job's suffering, which it does not.

A woe against the one who amasses what is not his and builds his house by unjust gain. The prophet promises that his victims will rise up as a taunt. It is close to verses 19 and 27, and it shows that ill-gotten wealth being turned against its owner is a recognised prophetic theme.

Jesus tells of a rich man who stores his harvest, tells himself to take it easy, and hears God say 'You fool! This very night your life will be required of you.' It has the same rhythm as verses 20 to 23, plenty followed by sudden distress, but the parable adds being rich toward God.

James speaks to the rich whose gold is corroded and whose unpaid wages cry out against them. It closely matches Zophar's picture in verse 19, and it shows the New Testament taking the warning seriously as an address to the rich, not as a way of reading a poor man's misfortune.

God tells Eliphaz that His wrath is kindled against him and his two friends because they have not spoken about Him accurately. That includes Zophar's speech here. The book's final verdict on this chapter is that its portrait of God is incomplete, however true its images about sin's poison.

The LORD sends venomous snakes among a rebellious people, and those who look at the bronze snake on a pole live. It is the biblical counterpart to Zophar's cobra poison: there is a real deadly venom, and there is also a remedy that God Himself provides, which Zophar never mentions.

study.oneStory:
Zophar's picture answers a very old question, which is why wrongdoing does not simply pay. Genesis 3 is already the story of a sweet-looking fruit that brought a curse, and Cain's blood-guilt in Genesis 4 shows the ground itself taking up the victim's cause. Zophar's world, in which the heavens and the earth bear witness against the wicked, is that world. The prophets and the wisdom writers pick up the same theme: sin is a poison that works from within, and the LORD sees how the poor are treated.

The passage also sets up what comes next. Zophar's confidence is answered in the very next chapter, where Job lists the wicked who die in comfort, and in the end by God from the whirlwind. The book uses him to show that the doctrine of retribution is true but cannot be the whole account of God and suffering. That leaves a question the rest of Scripture keeps asking: where is justice when the wicked seem to escape, and where is mercy for the sufferer who is not wicked? The Psalms and Habakkuk wrestle with it, and the New Testament answers it not with a formula but with a day and a person, Acts 17:31.

The answer comes to rest in Christ. The one who suffered without any oppression in Him took the cup that Zophar says belongs to the oppressor, Matthew 26:39. On that cross the world's sweetness and bitterness came together, and because He drank it, the venom of sin no longer has the last word over those who look to Him, as Israel looked at the lifted serpent, John 3:14-15. Believers are then set free from the need to judge one another, and are told to leave vengeance to God, Romans 12:19.

The story ends in the new creation with no oppressor and no poison. The book of Revelation describes the final removal of everything that spoils, 'no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4, and the Lord who exposes hidden wrong, Revelation 20:12, is the same Lord who wipes every tear. Zophar's promise that wrongdoing will not last is finally kept, though not in the way he thought, and not against the man he thought.

quiz.q: What provokes Zophar to speak again in this chapter?

options.text: He feels insulted by Job's earlier warning that his accusers should themselves fear coming judgment, and his agitated thoughts compel him to reply.
options.note: Zophar's opening words in 20:2-3 describe being personally stung by Job's rebuke at the close of chapter 19.

options.text: He has heard a rebuke that insults him, and the turmoil within him demands some kind of answer.
options.note: A close paraphrase of Zophar's own words, though less specific than naming exactly what provoked him, Job's warning at the end of chapter 19.

options.text: Bildad has asked him to clarify an earlier point.
options.note: Zophar's speech is a direct response to Job's own words at the end of chapter 19, not a request from Bildad.

options.text: He has just received news of Job's restoration.
options.note: No restoration has yet occurred in the narrative; that comes only at the book's very end, in chapter 42.

quiz.q: What is Zophar's central extended image in verses 12-16?

options.text: Sin that is sweet in the mouth but sours into the venom of cobras in the stomach, forcing the wicked man to vomit up his ill-gotten gain.
options.note: This vivid, visceral metaphor dominates the middle of Zophar's speech and captures the friends' core conviction about sin's ultimate self-destruction.

options.text: Stolen wealth that God eventually forces back out of the wicked man, leaving him unable to enjoy what he gained.
options.note: A true summary of the outcome Zophar describes, though less vivid than his exact image of sweetness turning to serpent's venom.

options.text: A wedding feast that never ends.
options.note: Zophar does mention rivers of honey and cream the wicked man will not enjoy, but his dominant image is about poison and forced loss, not an unending feast.

options.text: A shepherd carefully tending his flock through a storm.
options.note: No such pastoral image appears in this speech; Zophar's imagery here is one of poison and forced vomiting.

quiz.q: How does Zophar describe the wicked man's ultimate fate in 20:26-29?

options.text: The heavens will expose his iniquity, a fire will consume his tent, and his possessions will be swept away on the day of God's wrath, called his appointed inheritance from God.
options.note: This closing section pictures total, cosmic exposure and judgment as the wicked man's due portion.

options.text: Terrors and a piercing weapon will overtake him, and total darkness is reserved for his treasures.
options.note: A true detail from the same closing section, though less complete than the fuller picture of cosmic exposure and God's wrath.

options.text: He will be honored by future generations.
options.note: This directly contradicts Zophar's picture of exposure and judgment as the wicked man's true legacy.

options.text: He will be quietly forgiven without any consequence.
options.note: Zophar's picture is one of exposure and inescapable judgment, not quiet forgiveness.

quiz.q: What true, broadly biblical principle underlies Zophar's speech, even though his application to Job is mistaken?

options.text: That sin's pleasures are genuinely deceptive, promising sweetness but ultimately delivering death, a pattern Scripture affirms elsewhere, such as in Romans 6:23.
options.note: Zophar's underlying wisdom principle about sin's deceptive and destructive nature is echoed throughout the Bible's wisdom literature, even as his specific application to Job remains unfounded.

options.text: That ill-gotten gain, gained by oppressing the poor, cannot ultimately be enjoyed or kept.
options.note: A true, specific application of the principle from verse 19, though less broad than the general biblical pattern of sin's deceptive and fatal cost.

options.text: That wealth is always sinful regardless of how it is obtained.
options.note: Zophar's concern is specifically with ill-gotten, oppressive wealth (verse 19, seizing houses he did not build), not wealth as such.

options.text: That all suffering is proof of specific personal sin.
options.note: This is the flawed conclusion Zophar wrongly draws; the underlying truth about sin's deceptiveness does not require this false universal inference about all suffering.

quiz.q: How does the gospel answer the picture of God's wrath (chemah) that Zophar describes?

options.text: Christ Himself drinks the cup of God's wrath that sin actually deserves, so that those who trust in Him receive blessing rather than the judgment Zophar describes.
options.note: This substitutionary answer, seen in passages like Isaiah 51:17 and fulfilled at the cross, transforms Zophar's picture of inevitable judgment into an announcement of grace for those in Christ.

options.text: The wages of sin, which Zophar rightly senses are death, are paid in full by Christ on behalf of His people.
options.note: Correct in substance, echoing Romans 6:23, though less specific than naming the cup of wrath Christ drinks in the sinner's place.

options.text: The gospel has no relevant connection to this theme in Job.
options.note: The themes of sin's deceptive sweetness, its true wages, and divine wrath are directly addressed and answered in the New Testament's teaching on the cross.

options.text: The gospel teaches that God's wrath against sin was never real to begin with.
options.note: Scripture consistently affirms the reality of God's righteous wrath against sin; the gospel's answer is substitution, not denial of that wrath.

questions: Zophar's image of sin as sweet in the mouth but poison in the stomach is vivid and often true. What has looked appealing in the moment in your own life but proved bitter or destructive later on?

Zophar assumes Job's suffering must trace to hidden, ill-gotten wealth, with no actual evidence. Where might you be tempted to assume the worst about someone's hidden motives simply because they are suffering?
Zophar pictures God's wrath as an inescapable, burning judgment on sin. How does knowing that Christ bore that very wrath in your place change the way you think about your own standing before God?

Zophar calls the wicked man's ruin his rightful inheritance from God, twisting a word usually tied to blessing. Where do you need to remember that your own inheritance, in Christ, is blessing and not the judgment sin actually earns?

Zophar speaks his harshest words while feeling personally stung by Job's earlier rebuke. When you feel insulted or criticized, how do you guard against letting that sting shape your response to the person who hurt you?

translationNotes.note: The venom of cobras renders pethen, a greatly feared venomous serpent in the ancient Near East, intensifying Zophar's image of sin's stolen sweetness turning fatally poisonous once swallowed.
God will vent His fury upon him renders language built on chemah, heat or wrath, portraying divine judgment as an overwhelming, burning outpouring rather than a measured or gradual response.

Portion and inheritance render words, chelqah and nachalah, ordinarily associated with covenant blessing and land given to God's people; Zophar's ironic use of them for the wicked man's ruin underscores how completely, in his view, such a person forfeits any share in blessing.
